planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Bonanza was released in 2004 by the USDA Agricultural Research Service and the University of Nebraska Institute of Agriculture and Natural Resources, tested during development as Pawnee C3.

directions: Bonanza was bred through three generations of selection from Pawnee big bluestem specifically for improved in vitro dry matter digestibility, giving beef cattle better weight gains on well-managed warm-season pasture than its parent cultivar. It retains the broad Great Plains and Midwest adaptation of Pawnee while offering higher-quality forage yield, making it a strong choice for rotational grazing systems and warm-season pasture mixes. Like other big bluestem selections it also works well in conservation plantings and prairie restoration, forming upright blue-green clumps with turkeyfoot seed heads that color copper-bronze in fall. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in early spring before new growth begins.
sources: University of Nebraska Institute of Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Brush Strokes Little Bluestem (Powder-Blue Variegated Prairie Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Brush Strokes is a compact seedling selection bred from a cross of 'Blue Paradise' and patented under PP36206.

directions: Brush Strokes forms a compact, upright clump of dense, arching foliage marked with streaks of powdery blue that give the plant its name, turning a rich wine-red as autumn approaches. Bred from a cross of the popular 'Blue Paradise' little bluestem, it keeps a tighter, more restrained habit than the species and many older cultivars, making it useful in smaller borders and container combinations as well as mass prairie-style plantings. Fluffy silvery seed heads appear above the foliage in late summer and persist for winter interest and bird forage. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Little Red Fox Little Bluestem (Early Red-Blushed Prairie Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Little Red Fox was discovered as a seedling at a wholesale perennial nursery in Hebron, Illinois in 2019 and patented under PP36738.

directions: Little Red Fox carries fine-textured, blue-green foliage in spring that begins flushing with red highlights by midsummer, well ahead of most little bluestem selections, and deepens further into red, purple, and silver tones as autumn nights turn cool. It was found as a chance seedling at an Illinois wholesale nursery and has proven stable and true to type through more than a thousand vegetative divisions during trialing. Its compact, upright habit and early, long-lasting color make it a strong accent for mixed borders and mass prairie-style plantings alike, with fluffy silvery seed heads adding late-season and winter interest. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Wisconsin Strain Prairie Dropseed (Regional Native Selection)

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Wisconsin Strain is a regional selection of prairie dropseed valued by nurseries for its reliable early bloom and garden-worthy form.

directions: Wisconsin Strain is slow to establish in its first year or two before its extensive root system takes hold, so keep young plantings weeded and watered. Selected from wild populations in Wisconsin prairie remnants, it forms the classic neat, fine-textured fountain of glossy, hair-thin green leaves that turns bright orange to copper in fall, with airy, fragrant seed panicles in late summer often compared to the scent of popcorn or coriander. It is prized among nursery growers as a dependable, true-to-type source of prairie dropseed for formal border edging, mass planting, and prairie-style gardens, holding its shape through winter without staking or division. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes each spring.

common_name: Iron Cutter Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Fast-Spreading Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as sod, sprigs, or plugs from spring through midsummer, since Iron Cutter is a sterile hybrid propagated only vegetatively; it was bred on the cold plains of Oklahoma for winter survival alongside warm-climate performance.

directions: Lay sod or set sprigs into a full-sun site in warm weather and water frequently for the first two to three weeks to knit the stand together, then shift to deep, infrequent irrigation. Iron Cutter is the product of a decade-long breeding collaboration involving Dr. Charles Taliaferro, Johnson Seed Company, and MVP Genetics, selected for rapid spring green-up, dense fast-spreading growth, and quick recovery from wear, making it popular for athletic fields and golf course fairways and roughs as well as home lawns. Its dark green color and vigorous rhizome and stolon growth let it recover quickly from traffic and divot damage, but like other hybrid bermudagrasses it needs full sun and consistent fertility to hold its density against weeds.

common_name: DT-1 Bermudagrass (Drought-Tolerant Triploid Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as sod, sprigs, or plugs from spring through midsummer, since DT-1 is a sterile triploid hybrid propagated only vegetatively; it was co-released by the University of Georgia and USDA Agricultural Research Service in 2014 after drought-stress trials across five states.

directions: Lay sod or set sprigs into a full-sun site in warm weather and water frequently for the first two to three weeks to knit the stand together, then shift to deep, infrequent irrigation. DT-1 was bred in Tifton, Georgia and most closely resembles the widely planted Tifway 419, but was selected specifically for significantly better drought tolerance during establishment along with improved initial wear tolerance and faster recovery from traffic damage. It is generally faster growing than older commercial hybrid bermudagrass releases and holds turf cover and green color later into fall, making it a strong choice for sports fields and golf courses in hot, drought-prone regions.
sources: University of Georgia Turfgrass Breeding Program

common_name: Lobo Zoysia Grass (Fast-Establishing Low-Input Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish only from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 65°F; Lobo was developed by North Carolina State University's turfgrass breeding program from a 2014 cross of 'Meyer' zoysiagrass and the Z. japonica x matrella hybrid 'Victoria', released in 2021 and registered as 'XZ 14069'.

directions: Lobo is an NC State University zoysiagrass release selected from hundreds of nursery mates for an unusual combination of aggressive establishment and stress tolerance, traits confirmed over six years of multi-location, low-input trials including National Turfgrass Evaluation Program sites from Florida to New Mexico. It establishes and spreads faster than most zoysiagrass cultivars, holds good color and density under low mowing, fertility, and irrigation inputs, and has been a top performer in roadside plantings as well as golf course roughs and low-maintenance home lawns. Install only from sod or plugs, irrigate closely through establishment, and mow regularly once rooted in to maintain a dense, medium-fine turf.
sources: NC State University Crop and Soil Sciences
